% Generated by code/fees/WritePaper.py from transaction-fees-v1.
Finally, we asked whether trading costs changed the spread of selling or
its financial consequences, repeating the paired rule switch with fees
charged on completed orders. With technical traders held, the Sell
fraction at every step and the final grid were identical across all four
fee rates and three dealer depths for each starting market and fraction,
because fees did not enter any decision rule.
With technical traders active and fraction $f=0.20$, the Sell-majority
probability across fee rates was 1.00 at dealer depth $h=0.1$, 0.98--1.00 at $h=1$, and 1.00 at $h=100$
(Supplementary Table~\ref{tab:transaction-fees}). Nearer the crossover,
at fraction $f=0.175$ and dealer depth $h=100$, the probability changed
from 0.50 without a fee to 0.40 at 25 basis points. The paired
difference was -0.10 with a 95\% interval of [-0.28, 0.08],
so its direction was not resolved. The effect of fees on price declines
depended on the condition. At dealer depth $h=100$ and fraction $f=0.20$,
a 25-basis-point fee lowered the median maximum drawdown from 25.15\% to
23.67\%, a median paired change of -1.34 percentage points with a
95\% interval of [-1.60, -1.16]. At dealer depth $h=1$ and fraction
$f=0.175$, the same fee raised it from 76.52\% to 92.81\%, a
median paired change of 9.04 percentage points with a 95\% interval of
[3.46, 16.98]. Over a complete run, the fees accumulated: at 25 basis
points, dealer depth $h=100$, and fraction $f=0.20$, the median
cumulative fee income of the dealer was 36.19\% of the traders' initial
cash (Supplementary Table~\ref{tab:transaction-fees}). Thus, fees reduced
the price decline in some conditions and deepened it in others, and
because fees did not enter any decision rule, they could change interior
decisions only through active technical traders responding to the price.
